cards.explanation: The answer is False. The workers had a pattern to follow. The tabernacle was constructed exactly as God had directed Moses, Israel's leader, according to the pattern he had seen. No freelancing and no "ooh, what if we add a little something." I respect that, friends, because every time I add a little something to a batch, the oven files a complaint.

The answer is David. David, king of Israel (2 Samuel 5:3), is the one. The tabernacle remained until the time of David (Acts 7:45). That's a long run for a tent, friends. I've seen cookie sheets retire sooner.

The answer is Solomon. Solomon, David's son (2 Samuel 12:24) and Israel's king (1 Kings 1:39), is the builder. Stephen says it plainly: "But it was Solomon who built the house for Him." (Acts 7:47). David had the idea and Solomon did the lifting. That's like the friend who says "we should open a bakery" while somebody else gets flour all over the apron.

The answer is False. Stephen says, "…the Most High does not dwell in houses made by human hands." (Acts 7:48). Stephen had just mentioned Solomon building the house (Acts 7:47), so that line is a sharp turn. I'd have needed a minute to take that one in, friends, and I only have a mustache to hold my notes.

The answer is what house could be built for Him. The Lord says, "What kind of house will you build for Me, says the Lord, or where will My place of repose be?" (Acts 7:49). Stephen is quoting the prophet, and the question comes right after heaven is His throne and the earth is His footstool. When the throne is heaven, I'd be holding my little stamper and trying to look big.

The answer is the Holy Spirit. Stephen says, "You always resist the Holy Spirit, just as your fathers did." (Acts 7:51). He says they always do it, not just once. He puts the council right next to their fathers. That's a line nobody can nod along to.

The answer is True. Stephen says, "They even killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One." (Acts 7:52). He says it about the council's fathers. That's a heavy line, friends, and the room is hearing it live.
The answer is His betrayers and murderers. Stephen says, "And now you are His betrayers and murderers…" (Acts 7:52). It's a hard thing to say to a room full of people. Stephen says it straight.

The answer is that they have not kept it. Stephen ends with, "…you who received the law ordained by angels, yet have not kept it." (Acts 7:53). They received it, but they haven't kept it. That's the last thing he says before the room blows up.

The answer is Jesus. Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God (Acts 7:55). Right in the middle of the rage, he looks up and sees Him. I think that tells you where Stephen's eyes are.

The answer is False, and not even close. When Stephen says he sees heaven open, the council "…covered their ears, cried out in a loud voice, and rushed together at him." (Acts 7:57). Hands over ears is about as far from listening closely as you can get, friends.
The answer is spirit. While they were stoning him, Stephen appealed, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." (Acts 7:59). This part of the story is heavy, friends. Stephen turns to the Lord Jesus.

The answer is False, because he asks the opposite. On his knees, Stephen cried out in a loud voice, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." (Acts 7:60). The stones were still coming. I think that's one of the hardest lines in the whole book to take in.

The answer is True. Acts 8:1 says, "And Saul was there, giving approval to Stephen’s death." He's the young man whose feet the witnesses laid their garments at (Acts 7:58). He's right there when it happens.

The answer is God-fearing men. "God-fearing men buried Stephen and mourned deeply over him." (Acts 8:2). It comes right after Saul's approval of Stephen's death (Acts 8:1). They didn't just bury him, friends, they mourned deeply. I think that tells you how much he mattered to them.

The answer is that he drags men and women off to prison. "Going from house to house, he dragged off men and women and put them in prison." (Acts 8:3). That's Saul, and he's going door to door. He did it to men and women both. It's a heavy way to close out the passage, friends, and the text just says it plainly.
